steps.title: What investing is
steps.why: Before you invest a single dollar, it helps to know what investing is and when you are ready for it.

I'm completely new to investing.lead: Starting from zero is a great place to start. We will go slowly and explain every new word.

I know a little about investing.lead: You already know a little. This first step makes sure the base is solid.

I'm experienced with investing.lead: You have done this before. Pass the quick check on each step to skip ahead.

terms.meaning: Cash set aside for surprises, like a car repair or losing your job.
Debt that charges a lot of interest, like a credit card balance.

check.q: What is the one rule to remember before you invest?
options: Invest everything you have, as fast as you can
Only invest money you won't need soon, and keep an emergency fund in cash first
Wait until you are rich
check.explain: Right. Investments go up and down, so money you need soon should stay safe.

check.q: Why does cash kept under a mattress slowly lose value?
options: Prices rise over time, so the same cash buys less
The bank takes a fee from it
It doesn't. Cash never loses value
check.explain: Yes. That slow rise in prices is called inflation.

doIt.label: Emergency fund: I have one, or I know I should build one first
how: An [[emergency fund]] is cash you can reach quickly if something goes wrong.
It stays in cash, not in investments, so it is there when you need it.
No fund yet? You can still keep learning here. Just know it comes before investing.

link.title: National Bank: How to invest my money?

doIt.label: High-interest debt: I've dealt with it, or I have a plan for it
how: [[High-interest debt]] often costs more each year than investments can be expected to earn.
That is why many people deal with it before they start investing.
This is a readiness check for you, not a test. Tick it when you have thought about it.

coachPrompts: What is the difference between saving and investing?
How do I know if I'm ready to start investing?

steps.title: Your goal, timeline and risk
steps.why: A plan starts with what the money is for, when you need it, and how many ups and downs you can live with.

Save for a house or major purchase.lead: You are saving for a home or a big purchase. That goal has a date, and the date shapes the whole plan.

Prepare for retirement.lead: Retirement is far away, and that is good news: time is the biggest help an investor has.

Grow my wealth over time.lead: You want your money to grow over time. Let's turn that into a goal with a number and a date.

Generate passive income.lead: You want your money to pay you an income one day. Let's give that goal a number and a date.

I'm still figuring out my goals.lead: No clear goal yet? That's fine. Pick a practice goal here. You can change it any time.

terms.meaning: How long you can leave your money invested before you need it.

check.q: What is a time horizon?
options: The best time of day to buy
How long you can leave your money invested
How long the stock market is open
check.explain: Exactly. A longer horizon gives your money more time to recover from bad years.

check.q: You need the money for a trip next summer. What usually fits a goal that close?
options: Take as much risk as possible to grow it fast
It makes no difference
Take less risk, because there is little time to recover from a drop
check.explain: Yes. Short-term goals usually call for less risk.

check.q: Investments that can earn a lot usually...
options: Can also lose a lot
Are always safe
Are guaranteed by the bank
check.explain: Right. Risk and return travel together.

doIt.label: Write your goal card
how: Say what the money is for, in your own words.
Add the amount you are aiming for and the date you want it by.
We work out the monthly amount for you. The first number assumes no growth at all, so it is the safe one to plan with.

link.title: National Bank: 8 steps to build a solid investment portfolio

coachPrompts: How does my timeline change how much risk I can take?
What does my risk tolerance mean in practice?

steps.title: The building blocks
steps.why: Almost every portfolio is built from the same few blocks. Once you know them, fund names stop looking scary.

Low — I prefer stability.lead: You said you prefer stability, so we start with the steadiest block: GICs.

Cryptocurrency.lead: You have tried crypto. Here are the classic blocks that most long-term portfolios are built from.

I haven't invested yet.lead: You have not invested yet, so here are the three blocks you will hear about most.

terms.meaning: Management expense ratio: the fee a fund charges each year, shown as a percentage.
The list of things a fund owns, like the companies inside an ETF.
A short, plain-language document every fund must publish. ETFs have one called ETF Facts.
A scale from low to high that shows how bumpy the fund's past returns have been.

check.q: What is a stock?
options: A loan you make to a government
A savings account with a higher rate
A small piece of ownership in a company
check.explain: Yes. Each piece is called a share.

check.q: What is a bond?
options: A loan to a government or a company that pays you interest
A piece of a company
A type of bank fee
check.explain: Right. Bonds are usually steadier than stocks, with lower returns.

check.q: What is an ETF?
options: One single company
A basket that holds many investments at once
A guaranteed investment
check.explain: Exactly. One ETF can hold hundreds of stocks or bonds.

doIt.label: Read a fund page: find the fee (MER)
how: Open any fund or ETF page and look for its [[Fund Facts]] or ETF Facts document.
Find the [[MER]]. It is a percentage, charged every year.
You are only practising reading the page. You don't need to buy anything.

link.title: National Bank: 6 things to know about ETFs

doIt.label: Read a fund page: look at what it holds
how: Find the top [[holdings]] list.
Ask yourself: is it many companies, or a few? One country, or many?
A fund with hundreds of holdings spreads your money more than one with ten.

doIt.label: Read a fund page: check the risk rating
how: Find the [[risk rating]]. It goes from low to high.
Compare it with your own comfort with risk from step 2.
A higher rating means bigger ups and downs along the way.

coachPrompts: What is the difference between a stock and an ETF?
Where do I find the MER on a fund page?

steps.title: What it costs
steps.why: Fees look tiny, but they are taken every year. Over a long time they can eat a big part of your money.

ETFs or mutual funds.lead: You already own funds. This step shows you how to check what they cost you each year.

terms.meaning: Management expense ratio: the fee a fund charges each year, shown as a percentage.

check.q: What is the MER?
options: A tax you pay when you sell
The yearly fee a fund charges, as a percentage
The minimum amount you must invest
check.explain: Yes. It is taken from the fund every year, whether it goes up or down.

check.q: Two funds hold the same investments. One charges 0.2% a year, the other 2%. Over 25 years...
options: The difference is too small to notice
The more expensive fund always earns more
The cheaper fund leaves you with clearly more money
check.explain: Right. Small yearly fees add up to a big amount over time.

doIt.label: See what fees cost over 25 years
how: Type a monthly amount below.
Compare the two results: same contributions, same growth before fees, different fee.
Tick this off once you have seen the gap.

coachPrompts: Why do some funds charge more than others?
What fees should I look for before choosing a fund?

steps.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
steps.why: Spreading your money means one bad investment can't sink your whole plan.

Low — I prefer stability.lead: You said you prefer stability. Below, the calmer example mix is highlighted for you.

Moderate — I'm comfortable with some ris.lead: You said you are comfortable with some risk. Below, the middle example mix is highlighted for you.

High — I can handle significant market c.lead: You said you can handle big market changes. Below, the growth example mix is highlighted for you.

I'm not sure yet.lead: Not sure about risk yet? We highlighted the middle example mix. Look at all three and see how each one feels.

terms.meaning: How your money is split between stocks, bonds and cash. Also called asset allocation.

check.q: What does diversification mean?
options: Spreading your money across many investments
Putting everything into your favourite company
Changing banks every year
check.explain: Yes. If one investment does badly, the others can soften the fall.

check.q: A mix with more stocks usually means...
options: Less growth and fewer ups and downs
No risk at all
More growth over time, and bigger ups and downs
check.explain: Right. More stocks means a bumpier ride.

doIt.label: Pick an example mix to learn with
how: Look at the three example mixes below. The one that matches your risk answer is highlighted.
Pick the one you want to learn with and save it to your plan.
These are examples for learning, not a recommendation. A bank advisor can help you find your real mix.

options.name: Cautious
options.detail: Smaller ups and downs, slower growth.

options.name: Balanced
options.detail: A middle path between growth and calm.

options.name: Growth
options.detail: More growth over time, bigger drops along the way.

link.title: National Bank: What is an asset allocation ETF?

coachPrompts: How do I know if I'm diversified enough?
What is the difference between stocks, bonds and cash in a mix?

steps.title: Where your investments live
steps.why: The account you choose decides how much tax you pay on your growth, so it is worth picking with care.
steps.lead: Many beginners look at the TFSA first, because it is flexible. We put it first for you.

Save for a house or major purchase.lead: You are saving for a home or a big purchase, so we put the FHSA first. It was made for a first home.

Prepare for retirement.lead: You are saving for retirement, so we put the RRSP first. It was made for exactly that.

terms.meaning: Tax-Free Savings Account: your investments grow tax-free and you can take money out any time.
Registered Retirement Savings Plan: lowers your taxes today; you pay tax when you take money out later.
First Home Savings Account: helps you save for your first home with tax advantages.
The most you are allowed to put into a registered account. The government sets it.
Social Insurance Number: the nine-digit number the government uses to identify you for taxes.

check.q: What is special about a TFSA?
options: The bank guarantees it will grow
Growth inside it is tax-free
You can only use it to buy a home
check.explain: Yes. You pay no tax on the growth or when you take money out.

check.q: What is contribution room?
options: The most you are allowed to put into the account
The fee for opening the account
The least you must invest each month
check.explain: Right. The limits change, so always check official sources like your CRA My Account.

check.q: Which account was made to help you save for a first home?
options: RRSP
A chequing account
FHSA
check.explain: Yes. FHSA stands for First Home Savings Account.

doIt.label: Choose the account type to start with
how: Read the three cards below. The one that fits your goal is first.
Pick one and save it to your plan. You can change it later.
Many people end up with more than one account. This is only where you start.

doIt.label: Open your account
how: Have ready: a government photo ID, your [[SIN]] and your chequing account details.
The bank will ask about your goal, your timeline, your income and how you feel about risk. That is normal. It is how they get to know you.
Tell them which account type you chose: [[TFSA]], [[RRSP]] or [[FHSA]].
Before you add money, check your [[contribution room]] in your CRA My Account.
What happens next: the account opens empty. Nothing is invested until you add money and choose what to hold.

link.title: National Bank: Registered savings plans (TFSA, RRSP, etc.)

coachPrompts: What is the difference between a TFSA, an RRSP and an FHSA?
What do I need to open an investment account?

steps.title: A simple habit
steps.why: A small amount, invested every month without thinking about it, beats waiting for the perfect moment.

I haven't invested yet.lead: You don't need a big amount to begin. A small monthly habit is how most people start.

terms.meaning: An automatic transfer from your bank account to your investment account, on a day you choose.

check.q: What is compound growth?
options: A fee the bank charges every year
When your earnings start earning too
A type of account
check.explain: Yes. It is like a snowball that gets bigger the longer it rolls.

check.q: What does investing a fixed amount every month do for you?
options: It guarantees you will never lose money
It lets you guess the best day to buy
It means you don't have to guess the best time to buy
check.explain: Right. You buy a little more when prices are low and a little less when they are high.

doIt.label: Set your monthly amount and day
how: Choose an amount you can keep up every month, even in a tight month.
Choose the day. A good one is right after payday, so the money moves before you can spend it.
Save it to your plan.

doIt.label: Set up the automatic contribution
how: A [[pre-authorized contribution]] moves money from your bank account to your investment account by itself.
In your online banking, or with an advisor, choose the amount and the day from your plan.
Check which account the money comes from and which account it goes to.
You can change the amount, pause it or stop it whenever you need to.

coachPrompts: How does investing every month work?
What is a pre-authorized contribution?

steps.title: Staying calm
steps.why: Markets drop sometimes. Deciding now what you will do makes it much easier to stay calm later.

Cryptocurrency.lead: You have invested in crypto, which can swing a lot. So we moved this step up for you.

Low — I prefer stability.lead: You prefer stability, so drops may feel extra hard. A rule written in advance really helps.

terms.meaning: Fear of missing out: the urge to buy something because everyone is talking about it.

check.q: What is volatility?
options: How bumpy the ride is: how much prices go up and down
A fee for selling
A promise that prices will rise
check.explain: Yes. Some bumps are a normal part of investing.

check.q: What happens when someone sells in a panic at the bottom of a drop?
options: They avoid all losses
Nothing changes
They lock in their losses
check.explain: Right. Markets have recovered in the past, though there is never a guarantee.

check.q: Everyone online is excited about one investment. A good first move is to...
options: Buy quickly before it is too late
Slow down and check it against your plan
Borrow money to buy more
check.explain: Yes. That rush to join in is [[FOMO]], and your plan is the cure.

doIt.label: Write a rule for myself
how: Finish the sentence below in your own words.
Keep it simple, so you can follow it on a bad day.
We save it to your plan and show it back to you when markets get scary.

link.title: National Bank: Market volatility, what should you do?

coachPrompts: What usually happens after a big market drop?
How can I avoid buying something just because of hype?

steps.title: Practise
steps.why: Looking at a pretend portfolio is a safe way to use what you learned, with no real money.
steps.lead: Time to try it out. The demo portfolios use pretend clients and real past prices.

doIt.label: Open a demo portfolio
how: Go to My Portfolio and log in as one of the pretend clients.
Sofia's portfolio is a good one to start with. See how many problems you can spot.
Look for the things you learned: fees, the mix, how spread out it is, and the worst drop.
This step ticks itself as soon as you connect a demo client.

coachPrompts: What should I look for when I read a portfolio?
What does it mean if a portfolio is too concentrated?

steps.title: My plan and what's next
steps.why: Everything you chose now lives in one place, with clear next steps to come back to.
steps.lead: You made it. Your choices from the earlier steps are saved in My Plan.

doIt.label: Open My Plan
how: My Plan shows your goal, your account, your monthly amount, your example mix and your rule for yourself.
Below that is a timeline: what to do this week, this month, every month and every year.
Come back once a month for a 30-second check-in.

coachPrompts: What should I do next?
How often should I look at my investments?
